_comment: The Firsts' front pages (ui-spec.md 4.18, G14). One entry per First, in race order; a pack shows the ones whose goals it has. Our own text, written from the real Firsts' facts, never from a real paper's page. A page's story is drawn with the game seed salted by the goal id, so every player reads the same page. Story ids are stored in printed pages: never rename or reuse one. Tokens: {agency}, {director}, {season}, {crew}, {commander}, {rival1}, {rival2}, {also} (the Firsts folded into the page, by name in quotes). A tie story serves two or more agencies at once: there {agency}, {director}, {crew} and {commander} are lists ('A and B'). The page never names hardware (design.md 2.9). Order of an article: lead, also (only when another First is folded in), rivals2 or rivals1 (only with that many rivals), close. FrontPagesTest holds the lengths.

firsts.caption: WATCHING THE SKY. Neighbours gather on a rooftop at dusk to see the new moon pass overhead, a radio held up for its signal.
brief: How to see it from your garden. Page 2.
Radio amateurs hear the beeps. Page 5.

stories.headline: {agency} puts a moon in the sky
stories.deck: First artificial satellite circles the globe every hour and a half; its radio heard around the world
lead: {season} — For the first time, something made by human hands is circling the Earth. {agency} announced last night that its satellite had reached orbit and was sending signals home.
Tracking stations followed it across the sky within the hour. It passes overhead about every ninety minutes, and on clear evenings it can be seen with the naked eye as a slow, steady point of light.
{director}, the agency's director, called it “a small object and a very large step.”
stories.rivals2: Officials at {rival1} and {rival2} offered their congratulations, and promised satellites of their own.
stories.rivals1: At {rival1}, officials offered their congratulations and promised a satellite of their own before long.
close: To stay up, a satellite must travel at nearly eight kilometres a second, so fast that it keeps falling around the Earth instead of back to it.

stories.headline: {agency} satellite in orbit
stories.deck: A steady radio signal from space; crowds gather to watch it cross the evening sky
lead: {season} — The space age began last night. {agency} has placed a satellite in orbit around the Earth, the first ever, and its radio can be heard by anyone with a good receiver.
In towns and cities, people climbed onto rooftops and into fields to watch for it. Radio amateurs recorded its signal and played it down the telephone to friends.
Scientists say the signal alone will teach them much: how it fades and returns tells them about the air high above our heads.
stories.rivals2: {rival1} and {rival2} both said their own satellites were “well advanced.”
stories.rivals1: {rival1} said its own satellite was “well advanced.”
close: {director}, the agency's director, thanked the engineers who had “worked every night for a year.”

tie.headline: Two satellites, one season
tie.deck: {agency} reach orbit in the same season, and the race to space begins
lead: {season} — Not one but two artificial moons now circle the Earth. {agency} each placed a satellite in orbit within days of each other, and the world's first space race is on.
Tracking stations followed both across the sky. Each passes overhead about every ninety minutes.
tie.rivals2: Officials at {rival1} and {rival2} said they would not be far behind.
tie.rivals1: At {rival1}, officials said they would not be far behind.
close: To stay up, a satellite must travel at nearly eight kilometres a second, so fast that it keeps falling around the Earth instead of back to it.
{director} each thanked their engineers, and each claimed, politely, to have been first by a few hours.

firsts.caption: INTO SPACE. The rocket climbs from its pad at dawn, carrying the first human being beyond the atmosphere.
brief: The pilot's home town celebrates. Page 7.

stories.headline: {agency} pilot rides a rocket into space
stories.deck: {commander} flies above the atmosphere and returns safely, the first person ever to reach space
lead: {season} — A human being has been to space and come back. {commander}, a pilot of {agency}, rode a rocket above the atmosphere yesterday and landed safely minutes later.
For a few minutes at the top of the climb the pilot was weightless, and could see the curve of the Earth against a black sky. Doctors who examined the pilot afterwards found no harm done.
The flight was too short to go around the world: the capsule rose and fell back, like a ball thrown very high.
stories.rivals2: Officials at {rival1} and {rival2} congratulated the crew. Both say their own pilots are training hard.
stories.rivals1: Officials at {rival1} congratulated the crew and said their own pilots were “ready when we are.”
close: {director}, the agency's director, said the next step was to stay up: to fly all the way around the world.

stories.headline: Up and back: {agency} reaches space
stories.deck: A short flight above the atmosphere, a safe landing, and a hero's welcome for {commander}
lead: {season} — It was over in minutes, but the world will remember it for centuries. {commander} of {agency} became the first person to fly into space yesterday, climbing far above the air before falling safely back to Earth.
The pilot reported by radio throughout, calm and precise. At the top of the arc the sky was black, the pilot said, even in daylight.
Engineers were most worried about the return: the capsule hit the thick lower air at high speed and was slowed by it, pressing the pilot hard into the seat.
stories.rivals2: At {rival1} and {rival2} the mood was grim. Both are said to have pilots in training.
stories.rivals1: At {rival1} the mood was grim. Its own pilots are said to be months away.
close: Asked what came next, {director} smiled: “All the way around.”

tie.headline: Two pilots reach space
tie.deck: {agency} each fly a pilot above the atmosphere in the same season
lead: {season} — Two agencies sent people into space this season, and both came home safely. {crew} flew far above the air on short flights and landed minutes later.
Each reported a few minutes of weightlessness and a black sky at the top of the climb.
tie.rivals2: Officials at {rival1} and {rival2} said their own pilots would follow.
tie.rivals1: Officials at {rival1} said their own pilots would follow.
close: The next prize, all agree, is orbit: flying all the way around the world.
Doctors found every pilot in good health. Weightlessness, for a few minutes at least, did no harm.

firsts.caption: THE FIRST HUMAN IN ORBIT. {commander} waves to the crowd at the recovery field, hours after the capsule came down.
brief: Tracking ship crew to be honoured. Page 3.
What a pilot eats in orbit. Page 6.

stories.headline: {agency} pilot circles the Earth
stories.deck: First human being in orbit lands safely; rival agencies vow to follow
lead: {season} — A pilot of {agency} has flown all the way around the Earth and come home safely, the first human being ever to orbit the planet.
{commander} rode a capsule into orbit, circled the globe and landed to a hero's welcome, the agency announced last night. Its director, {director}, called it “the day the sky became a road.”
stories.also: The same flight also takes {also}, another first for {agency}.
stories.rivals2: At {rival1}, officials said their own pilots were “not far behind.” {rival2} said its plans were unchanged.
stories.rivals1: Rivals were quick with their congratulations. At {rival1}, officials said their own pilots were “not far behind.”
close: To stay up, a craft must travel at nearly eight kilometres a second. Coming home, it must shed all of that speed as heat.
Doctors found the pilot tired, hungry and in excellent health. Weightlessness, which some had feared, troubled the pilot little.

stories.headline: Around the world in ninety minutes
stories.deck: {commander} of {agency} becomes the first person to orbit the Earth
lead: {season} — Breakfast over one ocean, sunset over another, and home before lunch. {commander}, a pilot of {agency}, orbited the Earth yesterday, the first person ever to do so.
An orbit takes about an hour and a half. In that time the pilot saw a sunrise and a sunset, crossed every time zone and reported by radio from above each continent.
stories.also: The same flight also takes {also}, another first for {agency}.
stories.rivals2: At {rival1} and {rival2}, officials offered congratulations through gritted teeth.
stories.rivals1: At {rival1}, officials offered congratulations through gritted teeth.
close: The most dangerous minutes were the last: the capsule's heat shield glowed white-hot as it slowed from orbital speed, and radio contact was lost, as engineers had expected.
{director}, the agency's director, said longer flights would come next.

tie.headline: Two pilots orbit the Earth
tie.deck: {agency} each send a pilot around the world in the same season
lead: {season} — The race to orbit has ended in a dead heat. {crew} each flew all the way around the Earth this season, and all came home safely.
Each orbit takes about an hour and a half, at nearly eight kilometres a second.
tie.rivals2: At {rival1} and {rival2}, officials said they would catch up.
tie.rivals1: At {rival1}, officials said they would catch up.
close: Longer flights come next: a full day in orbit, then several.
{director} each called the flight a beginning, not an end.

firsts.caption: THE EARTH FROM THE MOON. A view through the spacecraft's window, the Moon's grey horizon close below and home a small half-lit ball above.
brief: Silence behind the Moon: the long wait. Page 2.
Your questions about the Moon. Page 8.

stories.headline: {agency} crew rounds the Moon
stories.deck: First people to leave the Earth behind fly around the Moon and return safely
lead: {season} — For the first time, human beings have travelled to another world. {crew} of {agency} flew around the Moon and splashed down safely yesterday.
The trip there took about three days. Behind the Moon, cut off from every radio on Earth, the crew saw its far side, which no human eye had seen before.
stories.also: The same flight also takes {also}, another first for {agency}.
stories.rivals2: At {rival1} and {rival2}, the news was received in silence. Both are known to be aiming for the Moon.
stories.rivals1: At {rival1}, the news was received in silence. It is known to be aiming for the Moon.
close: Coming home, the capsule hit the air at about eleven kilometres a second, faster than any craft returning from orbit.
{director}, the agency's director, said only: “Next time, we land.”

stories.headline: Earth seen from the Moon
stories.deck: {agency} crew flies around the Moon and brings home pictures of a small blue Earth
lead: {season} — The Earth looks small from the Moon. {crew}, flying for {agency}, came back yesterday from the first journey around another world.
Nearly four hundred thousand kilometres from home, the crew watched the Earth rise over the Moon's grey horizon.
stories.also: The same flight also takes {also}, another first for {agency}.
stories.rivals2: {rival1} and {rival2} both said they would land where others had only looked.
stories.rivals1: {rival1} said it would land where others had only looked.
close: The return was the hardest part: the capsule had to meet the air at just the right angle, too steep to survive or too shallow to stay.
{director} called the flight “the longest trip any of us will ever take, so far.”

tie.headline: Two crews fly around the Moon
tie.deck: {agency} each send a crew around the Moon in the same season
lead: {season} — Two crews flew around the Moon this season, and all came home. {crew} each saw the Moon's far side and the Earth rising over its horizon.
Each trip took about a week, there and back.
tie.rivals2: {rival1} and {rival2} said they meant to land.
close: Coming home, each capsule met the air at about eleven kilometres a second, faster than any craft returning from orbit.
The only prize left in the race, all agree, is a landing.

firsts.caption: ON THE MOON. The first pictures sent home from the lunar surface: an astronaut beside the landing craft, long shadows across the dust.
brief: A night of television: the world watched. Page 2.
What the Moon rocks may tell us. Page 9.

stories.headline: {agency} lands on the Moon
stories.deck: {crew} walk on another world and return safely; the race to the Moon is won
lead: {season} — Human beings have walked on the Moon. {crew} of {agency} landed on its surface, stepped out onto the grey dust and came home safely, ending the greatest race in history.
Millions watched the first steps on television, grainy and ghostly, sent across nearly four hundred thousand kilometres.
On the Moon everything weighs a sixth of what it does on Earth. The crew moved in long, bounding steps, collected rocks and dust, and set up instruments that will keep working after they have gone.
stories.also: The same flight also takes {also}, another first for {agency}.
stories.rivals2: Even at {rival1} and {rival2}, where the defeat stings, engineers stopped work to watch.
stories.rivals1: Even at {rival1}, where the defeat stings, engineers stopped work to watch.
close: {director}, the agency's director, could barely speak: “We went. We came back. That is all of it.”

stories.headline: Footprints on the Moon
stories.deck: {agency} crew lands, walks the surface and returns: humanity's first visit to another world
lead: {season} — There are footprints on the Moon, and with no wind or rain there they may last a million years. {crew} of {agency} landed yesterday and walked on its surface before flying home.
The landing was the most dangerous part: the craft came down on its engine alone, steered by hand over a field of boulders, with fuel for only seconds more.
Back in orbit, the lander met the ship waiting for it, and the crew began the three-day trip home.
stories.also: The same flight also takes {also}, another first for {agency}.
stories.rivals2: At {rival1} and {rival2}, the race is over. What comes next is not yet clear.
stories.rivals1: At {rival1}, the race is over. What comes next is not yet clear.
close: {director} thanked “every person who built, tested, tracked and hoped.”

tie.headline: Two crews land on the Moon
tie.deck: {agency} each land a crew on the Moon in the same season
lead: {season} — The race to the Moon has ended in a tie. {crew} each landed on the Moon this season, walked on its surface and came home.
On the Moon everything weighs a sixth of what it does on Earth. Both crews brought back rocks and dust.
tie.rivals2: At {rival1} and {rival2}, engineers stopped work to watch.
tie.rivals1: At {rival1}, engineers stopped work to watch.
close: Millions watched the first steps on television, grainy and ghostly, sent across nearly four hundred thousand kilometres.
Where the explorers go next, nobody has yet said.
